intro: To memorize pharmacology drug classes for nursing school, learn one rule per class, then test yourself on that rule over several days. Rereading a list of drug names rarely sticks. Testing yourself on what each class does, and why, does. This page gives you a Mac routine built on free tools, with the numbers on where nursing students and nurses get drug knowledge wrong.
tldr: Learn each drug class by its rule, such as what it does to the heart rate or blood pressure.
Quiz yourself with short cards spaced over days. Practice testing rates high in the research, rereading rates low.
Practice with invented patient cases too. Drug management was the weakest area in one Norwegian study.
Use Anki on Mac, which is free and needs macOS 13 or later, plus a one-page class table in Word or Google Docs.

blocks.text: Most drug class questions on a nursing exam do not ask for a list. They ask what a drug does, why it matters, and what you check first. So the memory work is different from the flashcards most students start with. Learn the rule for each class, then test yourself on it over several days. The rest of this page shows how to do that on a Mac, with free tools, and where the research says the effort pays off.
What weak drug class knowledge costs you on exams and on the unit

The cost shows up in two places. The first is exam points. The second is the moment on the unit when a drug name does not connect to a patient. A Norwegian comparison of 243 graduating bachelor nursing students and 203 registered nurses found medication knowledge of 61.5% for students vs 68.9% for nurses (p < 0.001). The gap was widest in drug management, where students scored 42.7% and nurses 53.2%.

Those numbers are not an exam score. They measure how often answers were correct in a study built for that comparison. Still, the pattern is clear. Drug management, the part where you pick an action for a patient, was the weakest area. Students gave 26.6% of their drug management answers with high risk of error, meaning they were confidently wrong.

A Spanish study of ICU nurses reviewed 87 admission episodes and recorded a global medication error index of 1.93%. In that study, 42.5% of 38 nurses failed more than half of a drug knowledge test. The authors used a small sample and an unvalidated test. They also did not report what share of errors came from knowledge gaps, so treat it as a warning, not proof.

The other cost is time. Hours spent rereading a chapter can feel like study. The research on learning methods rates rereading and underlining as low utility, with gains that are inconsistent and hard to apply well. You can finish a long session and still recall very little.
Why drug classes are hard to memorize

A class is a group of drugs that work the same way. The trouble is that the class name tells you little on its own. Students often memorize names in a list, then freeze when a question uses a different name for the same class. The class name is a label. The mechanism is the thing you need.

rows: Slow the heart rate and lower blood pressure. Follow your unit's hold parameters before giving one.
Relax blood vessels by blocking an enzyme. Watch for a dry cough and high potassium.
Block angiotensin II receptors. Similar blood pressure effects, and a dry cough is less common.
Lower cholesterol by blocking a liver enzyme. Ask about muscle pain and check your course text.
Reduce stomach acid. Check your course text for timing and long-term risks.
blocks.caption: Suffixes help you sort names. The rule still has to be learned for each class.

blocks.text: Notice what the table does. Each row gives you a suffix, a class, and one rule. The suffix tells you where a new name belongs. The rule tells you what the drug does and what to check. You can learn one row, then test it, before you add the next.
A class-first study method you can run tonight

Start with the mechanism, not the list. For each class, write one sentence on what it does in the body. Then write one sentence on what you check before the dose and one on what to watch after. That gives you three short facts per class. Three facts are easier to recall than a long column of names.

items: Pick one class. Do not start a new one until you can recall the last one from a blank page.
Write its rule in one sentence on paper or in a blank document.
Add two example drugs and one main side effect.
Close your notes and say the card out loud, then check it.
Schedule the next review for a day or two later, then later again.

blocks.text: Blank-page recall is the step most students skip. Testing yourself is the method the research rates as high utility, along with spreading practice over time. You will feel slower. That is normal, and it is the point of the exercise.
Set up Anki on your Mac for drug class cards

Anki's desktop app is free, and the Mac version needs macOS 13 or later. Anki lists separate downloads for Apple silicon and Intel Macs, so pick the one that matches your chip. The current version on the official site is 26.09.4. Check that page before you install.

Make one card per class, not one per drug name. The front asks one question, such as what the class does to the heart rate. The back holds the rule, two examples, and the nursing check. Press Space to show the answer, then press 1 to 4 to rate how well you knew it.

Anki also offers FSRS, an optional scheduler that replaces the older SM-2 method. Anki's deck options manual says it is enabled globally, not per preset, and that FSRS has been supported since version 23.10. You do not need FSRS to start. The default scheduler is enough for your first set of class cards.
Build a one-page class table in Word or Google Docs

A one-page table is your reference, not your study tool. Use it to check your recall after you quiz yourself. In Word, go to Table > Insert > Table on the menu bar, then choose the number of columns. In Google Docs, go to Insert > Table in Chrome, then pick the grid size. Keep five columns: Class, Rule, Examples, Watch for, and Nursing check.

Fill the table from memory first. Then open your textbook or course notes and correct it in a different color. The gaps stand out when you see your own mistakes marked. Do not copy a class sheet from a classmate without checking it. Sheets from another course or an older program can list different drugs or outdated rules.
Practice with patient cases, not just class lists

Drug management was the weakest area in the Norwegian study, so cases matter more than lists. Write a short case with an invented patient. Name the drug, the class, the check you make, and the reason to hold the dose or call. Then compare your answer with your textbook or course materials.

Use only invented or fully de-identified cases. Patient data belongs in systems your school and employer approve. Follow those rules before you paste anything into an AI tool, a flashcard app, or a shared document. If a rule is unclear, ask your instructor or your unit before you start.
Mistakes that slow down drug class memorization

items: Highlighting a chapter and calling it review. Underlining is rated low utility in the research.
Memorizing alphabetically. Alphabetical order trains spelling, not the rule.
Cramming the night before. Spreading reviews over days works better in the research.
Learning side effects with no nursing action attached to them.
Trusting one mnemonic without checking it against your course text.
Leaving the class off the card. The card should say which class the drug belongs to.

blocks.text: Most of these come from chasing a fast feeling of progress. Rereading feels productive. Testing feels slow. Choose the slower method, and track what you miss each day so the next session starts with your gaps.
What the NCLEX says about pharmacology, and how to check it

The 2026 NCLEX-RN test plan is effective from April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2029. Pharmacology sits under the Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies area. Secondary sources put that share at 13 to 19 percent of the exam. I could not read the official PDF to confirm the range, so check the 2026 RN Test Plan before you plan your weeks around that number.

Keep the test plan open in Chrome in its own tab. Press ⌘F to find the section you need, then match the drug classes in the outline to the classes in your program. Lazur sees what is on screen while you hold the shortcut, so you can ask about the open page. See [the Chrome assistant page](/apps/chrome) for how that works.
A week plan for drug classes

The seven-day plan below works on one class family at a time. When the table is complete for that family, repeat the cycle with the next family. Keep each session short and end it with a recall step, not a reread.
Edge cases and limits of this approach

Some classes break the suffix patterns. Some drugs belong to more than one class, and some combination products mix two. When a name does not match a pattern, look it up in your course drug guide rather than guessing. Read the full name before you answer, because similar names can look alike on screen.

There is little hard data on how much study time works. The research I found did not report study hours, grades, or how many students struggle with drug classes specifically. Treat these methods as well supported in general learning research, not as a promise about your grade.
Where Lazur fits in this routine

Lazur can help in a few specific ways. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a menu or button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Hold fn to dictate your rules at the cursor. Lazur drafts and types text, so check every row against your course material. You can also try [the Word assistant page](/apps/word) for setup questions.

Lazur does not learn the drugs for you. It does not click buttons or change settings in Anki, Word, or Google Docs. You still do the recall. Use Lazur for the setup questions and quick explanations, then close the screen and test yourself from memory.
Your first session

Open a blank document. Pick the class you missed most recently on a quiz. Write its rule from memory, then check it against your course text. Make two Anki cards from the gaps. Then stop. That is one complete session, and it gives you a place to start tomorrow.

faq.question: Should I memorize the full drug list or the classes first?
faq.answer: Start with the classes and their rules. Names fit onto a rule you already know. A full list with no rule is hard to recall and easy to forget. Add example drugs after the rule feels solid.

faq.question: How long should each study session be?
faq.answer: The research I found does not give a study hour count, so I cannot offer a sourced number. Use short sessions that end with a recall step, and review them over several days.

faq.question: Is Anki free on Mac, and which version should I use?
faq.answer: Anki's desktop app is free on all major platforms. The Mac version needs macOS 13 or later, with separate downloads for Apple silicon and Intel. The official site lists 26.09.4 as the current version, so check it before you download.

faq.question: Do I need FSRS in Anki?
faq.answer: No. FSRS is an optional scheduler. Anki's manual says it is enabled globally, not per preset. Start with the default, then try FSRS once your class deck is running well.

faq.question: Can I use AI to make my drug cards?
faq.answer: Check your school and employer rules first. Never paste patient data into any tool, and use invented cases only. AI can be wrong, so check every card against your textbook, course drug guide, and facility policy.

faq.question: What share of the NCLEX is pharmacology?
faq.answer: Secondary sources put it at 13 to 19 percent. I could not read the official 2026 RN Test Plan PDF to confirm that range. Check the NCLEX test plan page before you use the number in your plan.

faq.question: Does Lazur memorize drug classes for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains what is on your screen, points at controls, guides you through settings one click at a time, dictates text, and drafts text. You still do the recall, which is the part that builds memory.

costs.title: Exam points on drug questions
costs.text: Pharmacology is a named area of the NCLEX-RN test plan, and secondary sources put it at 13 to 19 percent of the exam. If your class map is thin, that share becomes points you give away across several questions. Check the official 2026 RN Test Plan for the exact range before you plan around it.

costs.title: Confident wrong answers
costs.text: In the Norwegian study, 26.6% of students' drug management answers carried high risk of error. Those answers were confidently wrong. A wrong answer you feel sure about is harder to catch than a blank. That is why the cost is more than a lower score.

costs.title: Hours that do not stick
costs.text: The 2013 review of learning techniques rates rereading and underlining as low utility. You can spend long sessions on them and remember little. The research I found gives no figure for study hours, so this cost shows up as lost time, not as a measured number.

costs.title: Medication errors and confidence on the unit
costs.text: A Spanish ICU study recorded a global medication error index of 1.93%. In that study, 42.5% of 38 nurses failed more than half of a drug knowledge test. The authors used a small sample and an unvalidated test. They did not measure how many errors came from knowledge gaps.

causes.title: Lists give you names but no rule
causes.text: A class list teaches recognition, not reasoning. You see a name and feel that you know it. Then the exam gives a patient, a lab value, and a new drug name, and the list does not help. Learn the rule that connects the class to the body, and the names follow.

causes.title: Names look alike across classes
causes.text: Drug names share endings and sound alike. Suffixes like -olol or -pril help you sort, but they do not tell you the action or the check. Students who rely on a suffix alone still miss the nursing step.

causes.title: Rereading feels like progress
causes.text: Rereading makes the page look familiar. Familiar is not the same as recalled. The learning research rates rereading and underlining as low utility and says the gains are inconsistent. Testing yourself forces the retrieval that builds memory.

causes.title: Drug management is a separate skill
causes.text: The Norwegian study scored pharmacology at 70.8% for students and 73.7% for nurses, which the authors judged not clinically meaningful. Drug management scored lower, at 42.7% and 53.2%. Knowing what a drug does is not the same as choosing an action for a patient.

causes.title: Knowledge stalls after the first working year
causes.text: In the Norwegian study, knowledge rose during the first working year and did not rise further afterward. The authors recommend more medication and pharmacology teaching in basic education, plus training beyond the first year. The gap does not close on its own, so you need a routine of your own.

causes.title: Classes have exceptions
causes.text: Real classes break their own rules. A drug can belong to two classes, and a combination product can mix two. Memorizing a rule as absolute makes you wrong on the one exception the exam chooses to test.

fixes.title: Learn the rule before the names
fixes.text: For each class, write one sentence about what it does in the body. Add one line about what you check before a dose and one about what to watch after. Only then add example drugs. The rule carries the class, so new names fit onto something you already know.

fixes.title: Recall from a blank page
fixes.text: Close your notes. On a blank sheet or in a blank Word document, write what you know about one class. Then check it against your textbook and fix the gaps in a different color. This costs nothing, and it is the practice the research rates as high utility.

fixes.title: Space your reviews over days
fixes.text: Review each class again after a day, then after a few days, then after a week. A paper calendar works if you do not want an app. Anki is free on desktop and handles the timing for you. Your memory works harder on each return, which is the point.

fixes.title: Test yourself with invented cases
fixes.text: Write a two-line case with an invented patient, a drug, and a question about the check or the action. Answer it in writing before you look at the answer. Drug management was the weakest area in the Norwegian study, so case practice targets the gap that matters most.

fixes.title: Keep one table and test both directions
fixes.text: Keep one five-column table for all classes. Cover the Rule column and recall it from the class name. Then cover the Class column and name the class from the rule. Testing in both directions forces more recall than reading the table top to bottom.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pick one class family
plan.text: Choose one family, such as beta blockers. Write its rule in one sentence and two example drugs on a blank page. Check the page against your textbook and mark what you missed.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Blank-page recall
plan.text: Close your notes. Recall the family from memory, then check. Write the gaps on a sticky note and keep it near your desk. Do this before you open any new material.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Make your Anki cards
plan.text: Make two or three cards from the gaps. One card asks for the rule, and one asks for the nursing check. Keep the deck small so reviews stay short.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Add the nursing check
plan.text: Add a card for what you check before the dose and what you watch after. Write the check in your own words, then compare it with your unit policy or course guidance.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Practice with invented cases
plan.text: Write one invented patient case for the family. Answer the drug, the check, and the action on paper before you look at the answer. Note the reasoning, not only the answer.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Review due cards
plan.text: Open Anki, press Space to show each answer, then rate it with 1 to 4. Redo the cards you missed on paper. Move on only when you can recall the family from a blank page.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Rebuild the class table
plan.text: Fill your one-page class table from memory. Compare it with your notes, then fix the gaps in a different color. Start the next week with the next family.
